rv.q: Ethically knotty exploration of protest and powerlessness
The play illustrates, with believable characters, the way grief can turn into anger, which in turn can sometimes shift uneasily between taking protest action and despair.
The politics of policing protest have left the building along with the sharper dialogue of the middle section of the play, melodrama, regrettably, crowding out drama.

The play as it stands is either too short or too long: not as concept, but when you pack in prison like a lighthouse flash and the gathering crescendo with accelerated narrative, the weight of it can evaporate.

Both performances are grounded and add to their characters’ likeability. Peiyao Wang ’s set is a circular, Ikea-pine-wood MC Escher-esque painting surrounding a patch of dirt. At times it felt that the actors found it hard to navigate, but it beautifully captured the cyclical nature of time binding them together as well as some of their arguments.

cn.t: An ambitious climate change drama earns praise for tackling neglected political issues but receives mixed reviews overall, with critics finding merit in its timely subject matter even as execution falls short of its aspirations.
